body.en:
• Software is far more than code: software = programs + documentation + configuration data + operating procedures - everything needed to install, run and maintain the system.
  • Unlike hardware, software is developed or engineered, not manufactured - there is no physical wearing out; it instead degrades through careless changes ('maintenance scars').
  • Professionally, software counts as the instructions (programs) that make hardware useful, the data those instructions process, and the documents that describe both operation and use.
  • The exam trap: "software = set of programs" alone earns half the marks - always add documentation and data.

• System software: serves other programs - operating systems, compilers, drivers, network stacks; close to the hardware and performance-critical.
  • Application software: solves specific business/personal needs - accounting, word processors, attendance registers.
  • Embedded software: firmware inside devices (ABS brakes, microwave, washing machine) - tiny, real-time and safety-sensitive.
  • Web applications: browser-facing sites plus cloud backends - continuous deployment, zero install.
  • Artificial-Intelligence software: systems that predict, recognise or recommend - built around data and models as much as code.
  • Domain choice shapes process choice: a firmware bug can crash an anti-lock brake, so embedded work insists on V-model rigour; a web shop can ship daily with agile cadence.

• Green hydrogen is produced by electrolysis powered with renewable electricity - its ecosystem of plants, pipelines, storage and fuel stations cannot run without software.
  • Role in production: software supervises electrolysers (temperature, pressure, current density), schedules runs against the solar/wind generation forecast, and logs the energy mix for 'green' certification.
  • Role in distribution: it optimises logistics of compressed/liquefied hydrogen - tracking tankers and pipelines, monitoring leak sensors, managing storage pressure and station inventory.
  • Matching supply to demand (hydrogen made only when the sun shines, delivered when buses roll) is a scheduling-and-control problem - squarely a software-engineering one, and a natural fit for AI-assisted forecasting.
  • Syllabus point to remember: hydrogen software blends embedded (plant controllers), system-level SCADA and web/AI dashboards - one project wielding several domains.

title.en: 1.2 Software Engineering: Layers and the Generic Process

body.en:
• Definition (IEEE style): software engineering is the application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software.
  • SE is built on four layers, like a pyramid resting on its tip's support: quality focus (foundation), process, methods, tools (top).
  • The process layer defines the framework - activities, milestones, when work products are checked.
  • Methods supply the how-to of each technical task: requirement analysis techniques, design notations, coding and testing practices.
  • Tools automate and enforce the methods (IDEs, version control, CI pipelines, case tools).

• Whatever model a team selects, five framework activities always appear: communication → planning → modeling → construction → deployment.
  • Communication: gather what customers actually need (requirements).
  • Planning: turn needs into scope, estimates, schedule and risk plans.
  • Modeling: analysis and design - model logic, data, interfaces before writing code.
  • Construction: code generation and testing.
  • Deployment: delivery, training and ongoing support. Then the cycle repeats via feedback.
  • Each process model (waterfall, spiral, Scrum...) is simply a different serialisation of these same five.

• Umbrella activities run parallel to and across all framework steps - they 'hold the umbrella' over the project:
  • Project tracking and control - is the schedule honest?
  • Risk management - what could hurt us, and what is plan B?
  • Software quality assurance (SQA) - are work products and processes up to standard?
  • Measurement/metrics - numbers about progress and quality for decisions.
  • Configuration & change management - one controlled copy of every artifact, every change reviewed.
  • Exam phrasing: framework activities advance the SOFTWARE; umbrella activities protect the PROJECT.

• Practical 2: define your project with a tight problem statement before touching models.
  • Shape: problem (what hurts), actors (who feels it), goal (what the system will do), scope boundary (what it explicitly will NOT do).
  • Example: 'Bus Reservation Mini' - let a student book a seat against posted schedules; NOT payments, NOT GPS tracking, NOT driver payroll.
  • A bounded scope lets you pick a sensible process model (Practical 3): tiny, well-understood scope → waterfall or a single increment; fuzzy scope → prototype; high risk + big budget → spiral; customer available weekly → agile.

• The grandfather model (1970): phases flow strictly downward - requirements → design → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance - each starting only after the previous gate-signs-off.
  • Strengths: disciplined documents per phase, obvious milestones, suited to fixed, well-understood scope.
  • Weaknesses: working software appears late; real requirements rarely freeze; a design mistake discovered in testing forces a painful climb back upstream.
  • Practical 1 board answer: waterfall drawing with its staircase - learn phase names in order plus one strength and one weakness each.
  • Pick it for: a college attendance upgrade where every rule is already on paper.

• Deliver the product in increments: the core product ships first; each later slice runs its own mini requirements-design-code-test and adds features.
  • Customers touch working software EARLY (like agile in spirit) and priorities shift between releases.
  • Risk spreads over slices - a slip on increment 3 does not endanger the v1 already live.
  • Fits staffing limits too: a small crew can finish slices one at a time.
  • Contrast with waterfall: same phases, but repeated per slice and delivering partial products each time.

• For customers who "know it when they see it": build a quick, cheap mock of key screens/behaviour, let the customer react, refine, repeat - then build the final system.
  • Loop: gather rough requirements → quick design → build/throwaway prototype → customer evaluation → refine requirements → (repeat until clear) → full build.
  • Flushes out hidden requirements early, when changing them is cheap.
  • Two dangers: the customer mistakes the fragile demo for the nearly-finished product, or the rush to re-use the throwaway code drags quick-and-dirty quality into production.

• Boehm's model (1988): the project sweeps outward in cycles, each loop split into four quadrants - planning, risk analysis, engineering, evaluation.
  • It is the first model to put risk front and centre: every round asks "what could sink us, prove it explicitly".
  • Early loops may produce only a paper spec or prototype; later loops produce increasingly complete versions.
  • Strength: ideal for large, expensive, risk-heavy projects. Weakness: heavier overhead - risk analysis needs expertise and each loop costs money; overkill for small classroom projects.

• A waterfall bent into a V: every development stage on the left arm pairs with a testing stage on the right arm - requirements ↔ acceptance test, system design ↔ system test, architecture (module design) ↔ integration test; the bottom is coding.
  • Test plans are written during the opposing build stage - acceptance test cases come straight out of the requirements document, long before any code exists.
  • Verification = "are we building the product right?" (reviews, walkthroughs); Validation = "are we building the right product?" (tests against user needs).
  • Favoured in safety- and audit-heavy domains (medical, aerospace) where each stage must be proven; inherits waterfall's rigidity for changing requirements.

• Agile (2001) answered heavyweight plans with four values: working software over comprehensive documentation; responding to change over following a plan; individuals and interactions over processes and tools; customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
  • The right-hand items still matter - the left are simply valued MORE.
  • Of the twelve principles, the heart three: satisfy the customer through early, continuous delivery; welcome change, even late; deliver working software every few weeks.
  • Others to quote: working software is the primary measure of progress; close daily business-developer contact; self-organising teams; regular reflection and tuning.
  • Practical 3 link: agile is the right model when requirements will evolve and the customer can review a build every sprint.

• Scrum organises agile work into sprints - fixed 2-4 week timeboxes, each ending with a ship-able product increment.
  • Artifacts: product backlog (every feature, prioritised by the Product Owner) → sprint backlog (committed slice for this sprint) → increment (potentially deployable outcome).
  • Ceremonies: sprint planning, the daily 15-minute stand-up (what done, what next, what blocks), sprint review (demo), retrospective (process tune-up).
  • Roles: Product Owner decides WHAT; Developers decide HOW; the Scrum Master clears obstacles and guards the process.
  • The iron rule of timeboxing: scope may slip, the deadline does not.

• XP pushes each good engineering practice to its extreme: if reviews help, review continuously - that is pair programming (two at one keyboard, one driving, one navigating).
  • Test-driven development (TDD): write the failing test first, then just enough code to pass.
  • Continuous integration: merge and run the whole test suite several times a day.
  • Refactoring: improve design continuously in tiny safe steps; small releases: ship thin slices frequently.
  • Simple design: solve today's need only; plus supporting habits - collective ownership, coding standards, 40-hour sustainable pace, on-site customer.
  • XP supplies the engineering discipline; Scrum the project rhythm - real agile teams usually blend both.

q.en: Define software.

a.en: Programs + configuration data + documentation + operating procedures - not just code.

q.en: How is software different from hardware?

a.en: It is engineered/developed, not manufactured; it does not wear out physically, though constant careless changes corrupt it.

q.en: Name five application domains of software.

a.en: System, application, embedded, web application, and AI-based software (green-hydrogen control software is a sixth in your syllabus).

q.en: Give an embedded software example.

a.en: The ABS firmware in a car - tiny, real-time and safety-critical.

q.en: What role does software play in green hydrogen production?

a.en: It supervises electrolysers, schedules production against renewable generation forecasts and logs the energy mix for 'green' certification.

q.en: And in hydrogen distribution?

a.en: Tracking tankers/pipelines, watching leak sensors, managing storage pressure and station inventory - matching supply with demand.

q.en: Define software engineering.

a.en: The systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to developing, operating and maintaining software.

q.en: Name the four SE layers in order.

a.en: Quality focus (bedrock), process, methods, tools.

q.en: Which layer is the foundation and why?

a.en: Quality focus - every other layer exists to protect the quality of the final product.

q.en: List the five generic framework activities.

a.en: Communication, planning, modeling, construction, deployment.

q.en: What umbrella activities span a project?

a.en: Tracking and control, risk management, SQA, metrics, and configuration/change management.

q.en: Framework vs umbrella activities?

a.en: Framework steps advance the software forward; umbrella activities protect the whole project while it advances.

q.en: What is a process model?

a.en: A chosen arrangement/serialisation of the framework activities - how work, reviews and releases flow.

q.en: Name five traditional process models.

a.en: Waterfall, incremental, prototype, spiral and the V-model.

q.en: Describe the waterfall model in one line.

a.en: Phases proceed linearly downward - requirements to design to code to testing to maintenance - with no return path assumed.

q.en: When does waterfall work best?

a.en: When requirements are stable, complete and well understood from day one.

q.en: Waterfall's biggest weakness?

a.en: Working software arrives very late; fixing upstream errors mid-way is costly and awkward.

q.en: What is the incremental model?

a.en: The product is built in slices: the core ships first, and each increment runs its own mini requirement-design-code-test to add features.

q.en: Why do customers like incremental delivery?

a.en: They use real software early and can re-prioritise later increments based on hands-on feedback.

q.en: When do you choose the prototyping model?

a.en: When requirements are vague - the customer will 'know it when they see it'; the disposable mock exposes true needs cheaply.

q.en: What are the risks of prototyping?

a.en: The customer may take the demo for the finished product, or throwaway quality may leak into the final build.

q.en: Explain the four quadrants of the spiral model.

a.en: Planning, risk analysis, engineering, customer evaluation - repeated outward until delivery.

q.en: Who should use the spiral model?

a.en: Large, expensive, risk-heavy projects; risk expertise is a prerequisite, so it is overkill for small projects.

q.en: Explain the V-model pairing.

a.en: Each build stage on the left (requirements, system design, module design, coding) pairs with a test stage on the right (acceptance, system, integration).

q.en: Verification vs validation?

a.en: Verification - building the product RIGHT (reviews against spec); validation - building the RIGHT product (tests against user needs).

q.en: Which model writes acceptance tests from requirements, early?

a.en: The V-model - test planning starts opposite the corresponding build phase.

q.en: State the four Agile Manifesto values.

a.en: Working software over comprehensive documentation; responding to change over following a plan; individuals and interactions over processes and tools; customer collaboration over contract negotiation.

q.en: Name three core agile principles.

a.en: Early and continuous delivery of working software; welcome changing requirements; deliver working software every few weeks.

q.en: What is the primary measure of progress in agile?

a.en: Working software.

q.en: What is a sprint?

a.en: A fixed 2-4 week timebox in Scrum that ends with a potentially ship-able product increment.

q.en: Name Scrum's three roles.

a.en: Product Owner (decides WHAT), Developers (decide HOW), Scrum Master (removes blockers, guards the process).

q.en: What happens in a daily stand-up?

a.en: Each member answers: what I did, what I will do, what blocks me - in under 15 minutes, standing.

q.en: Product backlog vs sprint backlog?

a.en: Product backlog: every desired feature, prioritised; sprint backlog: the committed slice for the current sprint.

q.en: What if a sprint's scope proves too big?

a.en: Scope drops out of the sprint; the deadline never moves - that is timeboxing.

q.en: Name four XP practices.

a.en: Pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, refactoring (also small releases and simple design).

q.en: What is pair programming?

a.en: Two programmers at one keyboard - one drives (types), one navigates (reviews, plans), swapping frequently.

q.en: What is test-driven development?

a.en: Write the failing test first, then write just enough code to pass it; the suite grows with every feature.

q.en: Why does XP insist on small releases?

a.en: Thin, frequent releases keep the customer steering the product and keep regression risk tiny.

q.en: Scrum vs XP - one line each.

a.en: Scrum supplies project RHYTHM (sprints, roles, ceremonies); XP supplies engineering DISCIPLINE (TDD, pairing, refactoring).

q.en: Say a college bus-booking app must evolve weekly with user feedback - which model?

a.en: An agile model - Scrum with short sprints; scope is fluid and stakeholders are available.

q.en: A missile-control firmware with frozen specs?

a.en: Waterfall or V-model: everything specified upfront, verification-heavy, audits at each phase.

q.en: Requirements unclear and budget limited?

a.en: Prototyping - a cheap visible mock flushes out true requirements before real investment.

q.en: (Practical 2) What makes a good problem statement?

a.en: Problem, actors, goal and an explicit boundary of what the system will NOT do - the bounded scope.

q.en: (Practical 3) Task set for the incremental model?

a.en: Core slice first: minimal req-design-code-test, then repeat per slice; each slice is a deployable increment.
